# Survival analysis {#sec-survival}


::: {.callout-warning}
This chapter is still a draft and minor changes are made without notice.
:::

This chapter deals with regression models for time-to-event data with possible right censoring, which 
is common for survival data but also in other applications of statistics[^app] such as reliability 
theory and credit risk. 

[^app]: Time to failure of an electronic component, say, or time to default of a debtor.

Some of the notation in this chapter will deviate a bit from 
the notation used for other regression models, which is deliberate and intended to follow 
some of the standard conventions in the survival literature. 
The outcome variable will, for example, be denoted $T$ instead of $Y,$ which is 
also a natural notation for a time-to-event observation. 
The regression models are formed in terms of a linear 
predictor $\eta = X^T \beta$ based on the vector of predictors $X \in \mathbb{R}^p$ 
and a parameter $\beta \in \mathbb{R}^p,$ and the effect of the predictors on 
the survival distribution is then always through $\eta.$ 



## Outline and prerequisites 

@sec-intro-surv covers the basic definitions specific to survival analysis 
and motivates why survival (regression) analysis is special. It also covers the
basic nonparametric estimators of survival distributions. @sec-par-surv 
covers parametric survival models and likelihood based methods for estimation 
and statistical inference. The accelerated failure time models and the proportional
hazards models are introduced, which show two different ways that the linear 
predictor can affect the survival distribution. @sec-semipar-surv primarily 
treats Cox's proportional hazards model, which is the most widely used 
survival regression model. As the name suggests, it is a proportional hazards model, 
but the methodology is *semiparametric*. In this case it means that a baseline hazard
function is left unconstrained. @sec-res-surv introduces survival residuals, 
which differ a bit from residuals considered for linear and generalized linear models. 
These differences reflect that survival models do not target conditional expectations, 
but otherwise the purposes of the residuals for model diagnostics are the same. 

The chapter primarily relies on the following R packages. 

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| cache: false
#| code-fold: false
#| message: false
library(RwR)
library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(skimr)
library(broom)
library(lubridate)
library(survival)
library(splines)
```


## Introduction to survival analysis {#sec-intro-surv}

A typical application of survival analysis is to the study of survival of patients 
after an initial diagnosis. In such a study, patients are enrolled whenever
they are diagnosed with a given (serious, life threatening) disease. 
We refer to the time of enrollment[^baseline] as the *baseline*, and we note that 
the baseline for different patients can be different 
calendar times, and that the survival time is the time from baseline to death.
The baseline is thus time zero on the time axis of the survival time.

[^baseline]: For some applications, all individuals or units can have the same baseline, e.g., in an experiment on the longevity of electronic components, but in many applications the baseline calendar times differ among units. In credit risk models of time to default, say, the baseline could be the date of the loan application. 

The patients are followed for some period of time, and if they 
die during this followup period, their survival time is registered. 
At a planned calendar time the study ends and the status of each patient is registered, that is, 
we register if they died, in which case we know their survival time, or if they 
are still alive. 
All patients alive at the end of the study have *right censored* survival 
times. This form of censoring is sometimes called *administrative censoring*. 
Some patients might also have dropped out of the study earlier, because they moved or did not want to 
participate anymore, say. At the time they drop out, we say that they are *lost-to-followup*, 
and this also results in right censoring of their survival time. 

In addition to the, possibly right censored, survival times of the patients, 
we may collect additional data on the patients. We can then use some or all 
of such additional variables to construct a regression model of the 
survival distributions. But it is not clear that 
we want to model *expected* survival times, and the conditional expectation 
is often not[^reasons] the correct target of a survival regression model. 

[^reasons]: One reason is technical. Expectations rely on the tails of distributions, and with right censoring we do not get that information. 

Regression models for survival data 
thus differ from the linear and generalized linear regression 
models in at least the following two ways:

* There is almost always a *censoring mechanism*, and certain aspects of the
    data are consequently missing. We need to deal with this in the modeling.
* Survival distributions are skewed distributions on the positive half line. 
    It is often the *shape* of the distribution rather than the location of the distribution
    that is of interest.

The overall objective of a survival regression model is the same as for any regression model: 
how are the different predictors associated with the survival time. We might then have 
different more specific questions we want to answer. For example, to determine if the survival distribution 
depends on a choice of treatment (testing). Or we might want to quantify how strongly 
a predictor is associated with the survival outcome.

We might, of course, also be interested in prediction, which we often call *survival prognosis*. 
It is rarely of interest to make a point prediction of a survival time for an individual, 
but we might report a prediction interval (the interquartile range, say), or we might report 
probabilistic predictions in terms of an entire (conditional) survival distribution.

::: {#exm-prostate}

We will throughout this chapter use a dataset on prostate cancer survival, 
which is included in the RwR package as the dataset `prostate`.
The data is from a randomized clinical trial on prostate
cancer patients with four different treatments (one placebo and three
different dosages of estrogen). There are 502 patients in the trial,
and we will in this chapter focus on four of the variables.

* `rx`: Treatment encoded as a factor.
* `status`: Either the cause of death or indication that the patient was alive at the end of study.
* `dtime`: The censored survival time since baseline in months.
* `age`: The baseline age of the patient in years. 

There are several other variables included in the dataset, and among 
these are `sdate`: the date that the patient entered the study. 
We will not use `sdate` for modeling, but it is used in @fig-prostate-entry 
to visualize the data. For later purposes, the data is converted to a tibble.

```{r}
#| label: prostate-data
data(prostate, package = "RwR") # version >= 0.3.5
prostate <- prostate |> as_tibble()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-prostate-entry
#| fig-cap: "The entry date of the first 100 prostate cancer patients into the study, their follow-up time and their status at end of follow-up."
#| column: margin
#| warning: false
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-width: 3
#| echo: false
arrange(prostate, sdate) |>
    head(100) |> 
    mutate(index = seq_along(sdate)) |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = sdate, xend = sdate + months(dtime), y = index)) +
    geom_segment() + 
    geom_point(aes(x = sdate + months(dtime), y = index, color = (status != "alive"))) +
    scale_color_brewer("status:", labels = c("censored", "dead"), palette = "Set1") +
    ylab("Patient") +
    xlab("Date") +
    theme(legend.position = "top")
select(prostate, c(rx, status, dtime, age, sdate)) # This is deliberate
```

@fig-prostate-entry illustrates the data for the first 100 patients 
that enter the study. The figure shows their entry date (baseline), 
their survival time from that date and the status indicator when follow-up ends, 
indicating if they are dead or if the survival time is censored.   

Since the treatments were randomly assigned, differences 
in the survival distributions between the four treatment groups 
can be ascribed to the treatment alone. That is, the treatments 
can be interpreted as the *causes* of any such differences. We
will first of all be interested in testing if there are effects 
of treatment as well as estimating the magnitudes of such effects. 

There are other variables included in the dataset, such as 
age, and we could use these variables for two different purposes. 
We could use the variables for prognostic purposes, that is, for 
fitting regression models that give more accurate survival prognoses 
for individual patients. Another purpose could be to investigate 
*heterogeneity* of treatment effects, that is, to investigate 
if the treatment works differently on different subgroups of the 
patients. 
:::

### Survival distributions and censoring

A survival time $T^*$ is simply a non-negative random variable. We will denote 
its distribution function by $F,$ and if the distribution has density $f$ w.r.t. Lebesgue measure, 
we have 
$$
    F(t) = \mathbf{P}(T^* \leq t) = \int_{0}^{t} f(s) \mathrm{d}s.
$$ 
The corresponding *survival function* of $T^*$ is 
$$
    S(t) \coloneqq 1 - F(t) = \mathbf{P}(T^* > t) = \int_t^{\infty} f(s) \mathrm{d} s.
$$ 

In terms of $S$ we define the *cumulative hazard function* as 
$$
    \Lambda(t) \coloneqq - \log(S(t)),
$$ {#eq-cum-def}
so that 
$$
    S(t) = \exp\left(-\Lambda(t)\right).
$$ {#eq-surv-from-cum} 
If $S$ is continuously differentiable, $-S'(t) = f(t)$ is the density of the survival distribution, 
and the *hazard function* is defined as 
$$
    \lambda(t) \coloneqq \Lambda'(t) = - (\log S(t))' = \frac{f(t)}{S(t)}.
$$ {#eq-hazard}
[There are one-to-one relations between the distribution function, the survival function and the cumulative hazard function.]{.aside}

We can observe that 
$$ 
    \begin{align*}
        \lambda(t) & = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0+} \frac{1}{\varepsilon} \frac{F(t+\varepsilon) - F(t)}{S(t)} \\
        & =  \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0+} \frac{1}{\varepsilon} \mathbf{P}(T^* \in (t,t+\varepsilon] \, | \, T^* > t),
    \end{align*}
$$
and $\lambda(t)$ thus has the interpretation as the instantaneous rate of death at time $t$ given survival beyond time $t.$ 
We also note that
$$
    \Lambda(t) = \int_0^t \lambda(s) \mathrm{d} s
$$
which explains why $\Lambda$ is called the *cumulative* hazard function.

We will not observe $T^*$ but only 
$$
    T = \min\{T^*, C\} \quad \text{ and } \quad \delta = 1(T^* \leq C)
$$
for a *censoring variable* $C.$ We call $T$ the *right censored* survival time 
and $\delta$ the *status indicator*. The status indicator is $1$ if $T$ is uncensored and 
$0$ otherwise. To distinguish the distribution of $C$ clearly from the distribution of the survival 
time, we will generally denote its survival function by $H$ and its density by $h$ (if
it exists). That is, 
$$
    H(t) = \mathbf{P}(C > t) = \int_t^\infty h(s) \mathrm{d} s.
$$

### Model assumptions

We will generally consider $n$ observations and let $T^*_1, \ldots, T^*_n$ denote
the survival times and $C_1,\ldots,C_n$ the censoring times. We then observe
the right censored survival times 
$$
    T_i = \min\{T_i^*, C_i\}
$$
and the status indicators
$$
    \delta_i = 1(T_i^* \leq C_i)
$$
for $i = 1, \ldots, n.$ 

The vector of predictor variables is as elsewhere denoted $X_i \in \mathbb{R}^p,$ and we are generally 
interested in models of the conditional distributions[^cond-dist] 
$$
    T_i^* \mid X_i = x.
$$ 

An issue of particular importance for survival modeling is to understand *when* a predictor variable is observed. In some studies, 
some potential predictor variables are monitored throughout the study. Such variables as BMI and 
blood pressure might be recorded on a monthly basis, say. It is possible to develop a 
general time-to-event theory where predictors also change with time, but it is both technically 
beyond this chapter, and it is also conceptually challenging to understand and interpret 
such models correctly.

[^cond-dist]: Note that the target is the conditional distribution of the unobserved and uncensored $T^*_i,$ not the observed and censored $T_i.$ 

We will throughout assume that all predictors are observed[^observable] at or 
before baseline, and we refer to such predictors as *baseline predictors*.

The modeling assumptions across the different individuals are now straightforward 
modifications of A5 or A6 to the survival setup.

[^observable]: Or, as a minimum, observable at time zero.

**SA5:** The conditional distribution of $(T^*_i, C_i)$ given $\mathbf{X}$ depends only 
on $X_i$ and $(T^*_1, C_1), \ldots, (T^*_n, C_n)$ are conditionally independent given $\mathbf{X}.$

**SA6:** The triples $(T^*_1, C_1, X_1), \ldots, (T^*_n, C_n, X_n)$ are i.i.d. 

Since $(T_i, \delta_i)$ is a function of $(T^*_i, C_i),$ then either assumption 
implies the same distributional statement about the $(T_i, \delta_i)$-s as about 
the $(T^*_i, C_i)$-s.

An additional delicate survival modeling question is what to assume about the 
joint distribution of $T^*_i$ and $C_i$ (possibly, conditionally on $X_i$). 
Throughout, we will make the following assumption.

**Independent censoring:** $T^*_i$ and $C_i$ are conditionally independent given $X_i.$ 

Even though the assumption above is a *conditional* independence statement, 
it is known simply as "independent censoring". In the literature, 
"independent censoring" may refer to a slightly more permissive 
assumption (Definition III.2.1 in @AndersenBorganGillKeiding:1993), 
stating that information about censoring status at any given timepoint 
is not allowed to affect the residual survival distribution beyond that 
timepoint. For this chapter we will make the stronger, but simpler, 
independent censoring assumption as stated above. 

### The Kaplan-Meier and Nelson-Aalen estimators

If $T_1^*, \ldots, T_n^*$ are i.i.d. and if they were observed, we could define the empirical 
survival function 
$$
    \hat{S}^*_n(t) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n 1(T_i^* > t)
$$
as a nonparametric estimator of $S.$ Clearly, we cannot compute 
$\hat{S}^*_n$ if we only have censored observations. 
The purpose of this section is to 
introduce two nonparametric estimators of a survival distribution 
when the survival times are i.i.d. and independently censored[^ind-cens]. 

[^ind-cens]: In this section there are no predictors, and we effectively assume that $(T_1^*, C_1), \ldots, (T_n^*, C_n)$
are i.i.d. and that $T_i^*$ and $C_i$ are independent. 

To handle the censoring we introduce the *individuals at risk* at time $t$:
$$
    Y(t) = \sum_{i=1}^n 1(t  \leq T_i).
$$
It can be computed based on the censored survival times, and it counts 
how many individuals have survived to time $t$ *and are uncensored* at 
that time.  

@def-KM below gives the general definition of the *Kaplan-Meier* estimator 
of the survival function, but to motivate this definition, we
first suppose that there are no ties among the observed survival times, 
that is, where we have strict inequalities among the ordered survival times
$$
    T_{(1)} < T_{(2)} < \ldots < T_{(n-1)}  < T_{(n)}.
$$
Here $T_{(k)}$ denotes the survival time with rank $k,$ and we will 
denote the corresponding status indicator by $\delta_{(k)}.$ 
[Without censoring, the Kaplan-Meier estimator equals $\hat{S}^*,$ cf. @exr-empsurv]{.aside}

When there are no ties, and $T_{(k)} \leq t < T_{(k+1)},$ we can factorize the survival function as 
$$
    \begin{align*}
        S(t) & =  \mathbf{P}(T^* > t) \\
        & =  \mathbf{P}(T^* > t \mid T^* \geq T_{(k)}) \times  \mathbf{P}(T^* \geq T_{(k)} \mid T^* \geq T_{(k-1)}) \\
        & \hspace{5mm} \ldots \times    \mathbf{P}(T^* \geq T_{(2)} \mid T^* \geq T_{(1)}) \times \mathbf{P}(T^* \geq T_{(1)}) \\
    \end{align*}
$$ 
where $\mathbf{P}(T^* \geq T_{(i+1)} \mid T^* \geq T_{(i)})$ is the conditional probability of surviving 
from $T_{(i)}$ to $T_{(i+1)}$ given survival beyond time $T_{(i)}.$ 

Since $Y(T_{(i)})$ is the number of individuals at risk[^at-risk] at time $T_{(i)}$ 
and $Y(T_{(i)}) - \delta_{(i)}$ is the number of individuals that survive the interval 
$[T_{(i)}, T_{(i+1)}),$ we can regard 
$$
    \frac{Y(T_{(i)}) - \delta_{(i)}}{Y(T_{(i)})} = 1-\frac{\delta_{(i)}}{Y(T_{(i)})}
$$
as an estimator of the conditional probability $\mathbf{P}(T^* \geq T_{(i+1)} \mid T^* \geq T_{(i)}).$
This gives the *Kaplan-Meier* estimator for $t \in [T_{(k)}, T_{(k+1)})$
$$
    \hat{S}(t) = \left(1-\frac{\delta_{(k)}}{Y(T_{(k)})}\right) 
    \cdots 
    \left(1-\frac{\delta_{(2)}}{Y(T_{(2)})}\right) 
   \left(1-\frac{\delta_{(1)}}{Y(T_{(1)})}\right).
$$ 

[^at-risk]: Alive and *uncensored*.

We can write the Kaplan-Meier estimator in a slightly more abstract notation as 
$$
    \hat{S}(t) = \prod_{i: T_i \leq  t} \left(1-\frac{\delta_i}{Y(T_i)}\right).
$$ {#eq-KM-no-ties}


To define the Kaplan-Meier estimator that allows for multiple deaths 
at the same time (ties), we introduce  the *counting process* of deaths (non-censored events)
$$N(t) = \sum_{i=1}^n 1(T_i \leq t, \delta_i=1),$$
and the jumps for the counting process given as 
$$\Delta N(t) = N(t) - N(t-) = N(t) - \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0+} N(t-\varepsilon).$$

\index{Kaplan-Meier estimator} 

::: {#def-KM}
With the above notation, the Kaplan-Meier estimator is defined as
$$
    \hat{S}(t) = \prod_{s \leq t} \left(1-\frac{\Delta N(s)}{Y(s)}\right).
$$ {#eq-KM-general}
:::

In the infinite product above, all factors where $\Delta N(s) = 0$ 
are equal to $1.$ There is thus only a finite number of factors different from $1.$ 
When $\Delta N(s) \in \{0, 1\}$ we see that @eq-KM-general coincides with 
@eq-KM-no-ties. The definition allows for $\Delta N(s) > 1$
to correctly account for multiple deaths at the same time and thus ties among 
the observed survival times. 
[The function `survfit()` from the R package survival can be used to compute the Kaplan-Meier estimator.]{.aside}


Since the cumulative hazard function is $\Lambda = - \log(S),$ we can estimate it 
nonparametrically as 
$$
    - \log(\hat{S}(t)) = - \sum_{s \leq t} \log  \left(1-\frac{\Delta N(s)}{Y(s)}\right).
$$ {#eq-cum-by-KM}
But there is also a different, and direct, nonparametric estimator of the cumulative hazard function.
The logic behind this estimator is that for a *differentiable*
survival function $S$ and $t > s$ (but $t - s$ small),

$$
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbf{P}(T^* \in [s, t) \mid T^* \geq s) & = \frac{S(s) - S(t)}{S(s)} \\
        & \approx - \frac{S'(s)}{S(s)}(t - s) = \lambda(s)(t - s).
    \end{align*}
$$

By a Riemann sum approximation we see that 
$$
    \Lambda(t) \approx \sum_{i: T_{(i)} \leq t}  \mathbf{P}(T^* \in [T_{(i)}, T_{(i + 1)}) \mid T^* \geq T_{(i)}), 
$$
and if there are no ties, the conditional probabilities in the sum above can be estimated[^est-prob] as 
$\delta_{(i)} / Y(T_{(i)}).$ This leads to the *Nelson-Aalen* estimator 
$$
    \hat{\Lambda}(t) = \sum_{i: T_{(i)} \leq t} \frac{\delta_{(i)}}{Y(T_{(i)})}.
$$ {#eq-NA-no-ties}

[^est-prob]: Either $\delta_{(i)} = 1$ and one individual out of $Y(T_{(i)})$ dies in the interval (at time $T_{(i)}$), or $\delta_{(i)} = 0$ and no individuals die in the interval.

The general definition below allows for multiple deaths at the same time.

::: {#def-NA}
The Nelson-Aalen \index{Nelson-Aalen estimator} estimator of the cumulative hazard function is  
$$
    \hat{\Lambda}(t) = \sum_{s \leq t}  \frac{\Delta N(s)}{Y(s)}.
$$ {#eq-NA-general}
:::

Since the survival function is given by $S(t) = \exp(-\Lambda(t)),$ we can
estimate the survival function by plugging the 
Nelson-Aalen estimator of the cumulative hazard, which gives
$$
    \exp\left(-\hat{\Lambda}(t)\right) = \prod_{s \leq t} \exp\left(-
    \frac{\Delta N(s)}{Y(s)}\right).
$$ {#eq-surv-by-NA}

We note that $\exp(-\hat{\Lambda})$ is not the Kaplan-Meier estimator, nor is 
$- \log(\hat{S})$ the Nelson-Aalen estimator. 
[The function `survfit()` with argument `stype = 2` estimates the survival function in terms of the Nelson-Aalen estimator via @eq-surv-by-NA.]{.aside}

The mismatch between the Kaplan-Meier and the Nelson-Aalen estimators is a small nuisance, 
but we may note that 
$$ 
    \exp\left(- \frac{\Delta N(s)}{Y(s)}\right) \approx  \left(1 -
    \frac{\Delta N(s)}{Y(s)}\right)
$$
for large $Y(s)$ by using the Taylor expansion $\exp(x) = 1 + x + O(x^2).$ 
Thus differences between the factors are small unless $s$ is so large that 
the number of individuals at risk, $Y(s),$ is small. 

One can argue that the way ties are handled above presumes that survival times 
can be exactly equal, which is at odds with any continuous survival distribution. 
If we regard ties as a consequence of lack of precision in our registration or due to 
rounding of the survival times, it makes sense to replace $\frac{\Delta N(s)}{Y(s)}$
by 
$$
    \frac{1}{Y(s)} + \frac{1}{Y(s) - 1} + \ldots + \frac{1}{Y(s) - \Delta N(s) + 1}.
$$ 
[The function `survfit()` with argument `ctype = 2` will use the Fleming-Harrington correction for ties.]{.aside}
This is known as the *Fleming-Harrington* correction for ties. It often does not
make much of a practical difference though. 

::: {#exm-prostate-II}

We continue @exm-prostate by first considering a summary of the marginal distributions 
of the four variables. 

```{r}
#| label: tbl-skim-prostate
#| skimr_include_summary: FALSE
#| tbl-cap: "Data summary of the four variables in the `prostate` dataset."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
#| column: page-right
select(prostate, c(rx, status, dtime, age)) |> skim()
```

@tbl-skim-prostate shows 148 patients (out of 502) were alive at the end of the 
study. Thus 148 of the survival times are right censored. @tbl-prostate-death 
shows a more detailed tabulation of the values of the `status` variable, which 
specifies one out of nine different causes of death---in addition to specifying 
if the patient is still alive. We may also note that the survival time (`dtime`)
is registered in months since baseline, which is a very coarse scale. Consequently 
there are many ties in the data. 

```{r}
#| label: tbl-prostate-death
#| column: margin
#| tbl-cap: "Tabulation of different causes of death."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
#| echo: false
prostate[, "status", drop = FALSE] |> 
    table() |>
    knitr::kable()
```

We will fit a survival distribution, using either of the nonparametric estimators 
above, where we ignore the information about different causes of death. Thus 
the `status` variable will only be used to determine the censoring status.

We fit survival functions for all patients using the `survfit()` function 
from the survival package. See `?survfit.formula` for details about how to 
specify a model using the formula interface. Note that the left hand side of the 
formula, that specifies the outcome, uses the special `Surv()` function syntax 
to include information about the censoring status. We fit the survival functions 
below using both the Kaplan-Meier and the Nelson-Aalen estimators, and we also fit the 
survival function using the Nelson-Aalen estimator with the Fleming-Harrington 
correction for ties. 

```{r}
#| label: prostate-survfit
#| code-fold: show
prostate_KM <- survfit(
    Surv(dtime, status != "alive") ~ 1, 
    data = prostate,
)

prostate_NA <- survfit(
    Surv(dtime, status != "alive") ~ 1, 
    data = prostate,
    stype = 2
)

prostate_NA_FH <- survfit(
    Surv(dtime, status != "alive") ~ 1, 
    data = prostate,
    stype = 2,
    ctype = 2
)
```

@fig-survival-est shows the fitted survival curves---including a plot that zooms in on 
a part of the curves. The differences are small and barely visible, and they are most pronounced 
in the tail of the distribution. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-survival-est
#| fig-cap: "Left: estimated survival function for patients with prostate cancer using the Kaplan-Meier estimator (black), the Nelson-Aalen estimator (blue) and the Nelson-Aalen estimator with the Fleming-Harrington correction for ties (red). Right: the same as the left figure but zoomed in."
#| fig-cap-location: margin
#| opts.label: widefigure2
#| code-fold: true
p1 <- summary(prostate_KM, data.frame = TRUE) |> 
        ggplot(aes(time, surv)) + 
        geom_step(data = summary(prostate_NA, data.frame = TRUE), color = "blue") +
        geom_step(data = summary(prostate_NA_FH, data.frame = TRUE), color = "red") +
        geom_step() +
        ylim(0, 1) +
        xlab("time (months)") + 
        ylab("survival probability")

p2 <- p1 + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(50, 75), ylim = c(0.20, 0.40))

gridExtra::grid.arrange(p1, p2, ncol = 2)
```

We then fit a separate survival function for each treatment group. We can think about this as 
a simple regression model with a single categorical predictor variable (the treatment variable `rx`), 
and the formula specification below is similar to other regression model specifications. The 
main difference is that using `survfit()` we fit a survival function for each treatment group instead of a 
mean value, say. 

```{r}
#| label: prostate-surv-rx
#| code-fold: show
prostate_KM_rx <- survfit(
    Surv(dtime, status != "alive") ~ rx, 
    data = prostate
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-prostate-surv-rx
#| fig-cap: "Kaplan-Meier estimators of the survival function for each of the four treatment groups."
#| fig-cap-location: margin
summary(prostate_KM_rx, data.frame = TRUE) |> 
        ggplot(aes(time, surv, color = strata)) + 
        geom_step() +
        ylim(0, 1) +
        xlab("time (months)") + 
        ylab("survival probability") +
        theme(legend.position = "top")
```
::: 

## Parametric survival models {#sec-par-surv}

In this section we focus on parametric models of the survival distribution, 
and we will first derive a generic expression for the likelihood function. 
We then turn to regression models and introduce the accelerated failure time 
models and the proportional hazards models as two different ways for the 
predictors to affect the outcome distribution.

### The likelihood

Recall that in terms of $T^*$ and $C$ we have $T = \min\{T^*, C\}$ and $\delta = 1(T^* \leq C).$ 
Our first result gives the density of the joint distribution of $(T, \delta)$ in terms of 
the marginal distributions of $T^*$ and $C$ when they are independent.

::: {#thm-density-surv}
If $T^*$ and $C$ are independent the joint distribution of $(T, \delta)$ has density 
$$
    g(t, \delta)  = f(t)^\delta S(t)^{1-\delta} h(t)^{1-\delta} H(t)^\delta
$$
w.r.t. the product measure $m \otimes \tau$ (Lebesgue measure times the counting measure). 
:::

::: {.proof}
First note that
$$
    \begin{align*}
    \mathbf{P}(T \leq t, \delta = 1) & = \mathbf{P}(T^* \leq t, \delta = 1) \\
    & = \mathbf{P}(T^* \leq t,C \geq T^*) \\
    & = \int_0^t f(s) \int_s^{\infty} h(u) \mathrm{d} u \mathrm{d} s \\
    & = \int_0^t f(s) H(s) \mathrm{d} s.
    \end{align*}
$$
Likewise, 
$$
    \mathbf{P}(T \leq t, \delta = 0) = \int_0^t h(s) S(s) \mathrm{d} s,
$$
and we conclude that the density is
$$
    g(t, \delta) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
    f(t) H(t) & \text{if } \delta = 1 \\
    h(t) S(t) & \text{if } \delta = 0.
    \end{array} \right.
$$
:::

Based on the density result above we can introduce the full likelihood for right censored 
observations. With $(T_1, \delta_1), \ldots, (T_n, \delta_n)$ independent, 
$F_i$ the distribution function for $T_i^*$ and $H_i$ the survival function for the 
censoring variable $C_i$, the full likelihood is 
\index{likelihood!survival model}
$$
    L(F, H) = \prod_{i=1}^n  f_i(T_i)^{\delta_i} S_i(T_i)^{1-{\delta_i}} h_i(T_i)^{1-{\delta_i}} H_i(T_i)^{\delta_i},
$$
where $F$ and $H$ are shorthand for $F_1, \ldots, F_n$ and $H_1, \ldots, H_n$.

If the survival distribution can vary independently of the censoring distribution,
the full likelihood can be seen as a function of $F$ only, 
$$
    F \mapsto \prod_{i=1}^n  f_i(T_i)^{\delta_i} S_i(T_i)^{1-{\delta_i}} K_i 
    = \left(\prod_{i=1}^n  f_i(T_i)^{\delta_i} S_i(T_i)^{1-{\delta_i}}\right) \left(\prod_{i=1}^n K_i\right),
$$
with $K_i$ some constants depending on the observations but not on the survival distribution $F.$
For estimation and inference purposes, we can drop the factor $\prod_{i=1}^n K_i$ since it is 
only the first factor that depends on $F$. 

::: {#def-likelihood}
The survival likelihood is
$$ 
L(F) \coloneqq \prod_{i=1}^n f_{i}(T_i)^{\delta_i} S_{i}(T_i)^{1-{\delta_i}}.
$$ {#eq-survlike}
:::

For a parametrized model of the distributions of $T^*_1, \ldots, T^*_n$ we have that 
$f_i = f_{i, \beta}$ for some parameter $\beta.$ This gives the survival likelihood 
as a function of $\beta$,
$$
    L(\beta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f_{i, \beta}(T_i)^{\delta_i} S_{i, \beta}(T_i)^{1-{\delta_i}}.
$$

The survival likelihood is the likelihood we will use throughout this chapter. 
Its derivation made it explicit how this is a likelihood w.r.t. a dominating measure
up to a factor that depends on the censoring mechanism only. We can ignore 
this factor when it does not depend on the unknown parameter $\beta.$ 
The argument for that is not independent censoring[^ind-cen] as such
but that the $H_i$-s do not depend upon $\beta.$ Technically, the censoring 
distribution and the parameter $\beta$ are assumed *variation independent*.

[^ind-cen]: Though independent censoring plays a role here for our particular derivation and form of the full likelihood.

It is possible to take a slightly different point of view and
condition on the censoring variables instead. Then the dominating measure
for the $i$-th censored observation, $T_i,$ becomes Lebesgue measure plus a 
unit point mass in $C_i.$ One arrives at the same likelihood as above though. 

We can also express the likelihood in terms of the hazard and cumulative 
hazard functions.

::: {#prp-likelihood}
If $F_i$ is the distribution function of $T_i^*$ with hazard function $\lambda_{i}$ and 
cumulative hazard function $\Lambda_{i},$ the survival likelihood equals 
$$ 
    L(F) = L(\Lambda) \coloneqq \prod_{i=1}^n \lambda_{i}(T_i)^{\delta_i} e^{- \Lambda_{i}(T_i)} 
$$ {#eq-survlike1dot5}
::: 

::: {.proof}
Recall that 
$$
    \lambda_{i}(t) = \frac{f_{i}(t)}{S_{i}(t)}  
$$
and that 
$$
    S_{i}(t) = e^{- \Lambda_{i}(t)}.
$$
Hence 
$$
    \begin{align*}
    L(F) & = \prod_{i=1}^n f_{i}(T_i)^{\delta_i} S_{i}(T_i)^{1-{\delta_i}} \\
    & =  \prod_{i=1}^n \lambda_{i}(T_i)^{\delta_i} S_{i}(T_i)^{\delta_i} S_{i}(T_i)^{1-{\delta_i}} \\
    & = \prod_{i=1}^n \lambda_{i}(T_i)^{\delta_i} S_{i}(T_i) \\
    & =  \prod_{i=1}^n \lambda_{i}(T_i)^{\delta_i} e^{- \Lambda_{i}(T_i)} = L(\Lambda).
    \end{align*}
$$
:::

If $f_{i, \beta}$ is a parametrized density for the survival distribution with 
hazard function $\lambda_{i, \beta}$ and cumulative hazard function $\Lambda_{i, \beta},$
the likelihood as a function of $\beta$ can then be expressed as
$$ 
    L(\beta) = \prod_{i=1}^n \lambda_{i, \beta}(T_i)^{\delta_i} e^{- \Lambda_{i, \beta}(T_i)}.
$$ {#eq-survlike2}


:::{#exm-weibull-hazard}
The *Weibull distribution* has hazard function 
$$
    \lambda(t) = \alpha \gamma t^{\gamma - 1}
$$
for $\alpha, \gamma > 0$ two parameters. The special 
case $\gamma = 1$ gives us the exponential distribution 
with constant hazard function. The Weibull distribution 
has increasing hazard functions over time when $\gamma > 1$
and decreasing hazard function when $\gamma < 1.$

The cumulative hazard function is 
$$
    \Lambda(t) = \alpha  \int_0^t \gamma s^{\gamma - 1} \mathrm{d} s = \alpha t^\gamma.
$$

For right censored i.i.d. observations from the Weibull model, 
the likelihood becomes 
$$
    L(\alpha, \gamma) = \prod_{i=1}^n (\alpha \gamma)^{\delta_i} T_i^{\delta_i(\gamma - 1)} e^{- \alpha T_i^\gamma},
$$
and the log-likelihood is 
$$
    \begin{align*}
    \ell(\alpha, \gamma) & = \log L(\alpha, \gamma) \\
    & = \sum_{i=1}^n \delta_i (\log(\alpha) + \log(\gamma) + (\gamma - 1)\log(T_i)) 
    - \alpha T_i^\gamma.
    \end{align*}
$$
:::

:::{#exm-exponential-MLE}

## MLE for the exponential distribution

Continuing @exm-weibull-hazard and fixing $\gamma = 1,$ corresponding to an
exponential distribution with hazard rate $\alpha,$ we find that the 
log-likelihood equals 
$$
    \ell(\alpha) = \sum_{i=1}^n \delta_i \log(\alpha) - \alpha T_i
$$
up to additive terms that do not depend on $\alpha.$ Provided that at least one 
observation is uncensored, this log-likelihood has a unique stationary point 
$$
    \hat{\alpha} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \delta_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n T_i} = \frac{n_u}{\sum_{i=1}^n T_i}
$$
where $n_u = \sum_{i=1}^n \delta_i$ is the number of deaths (the number of uncensored events). 
The second derivative of $\ell$ is $-n_u / \alpha^2 < 0,$ so $\ell$ is strictly concave and $\hat{\alpha}$ is 
the MLE. 

If we had treated the observations as if there were no censoring, we would get the MLE 
$$
    \frac{n}{\sum_{i=1}^n T_i} > \hat{\alpha},
$$
which overestimates the rate. 

If we, on the other hand, discard the censored observations, we would get the MLE 
$$
    \frac{n_u}{\sum_{i=1}^n \delta_i T_i} > \hat{\alpha},
$$
which likewise overestimates the rate.
:::

### Regression models

We introduce two ways that predictor variables 
can affect the survival outcome distribution: the accelerated failure time 
models, exemplified by the log-logistic model, and the proportional 
hazards models, exemplified by the Weibull model. In the latter case, 
it turns out that the likelihood can be computed and optimized 
using methods for Poisson generalized linear models. 

#### Accelerated failure time models {.unnumbered}

::: {#exm-log-logistic}

## Log-logistic distribution

Suppose $Z$ has a logistic distribution with distribution function \index{log-logistic distribution}
$$
    G(z) = \frac{e^{\lambda z}}{1 + e^{\lambda z}}.
$$
The distribution of $T^* = e^Z$ is then the *log-logistic* distribution, whose 
distribution function is 
$$
    F(t) = G(\log(t)) = \frac{t^{\lambda}}{1 + t^{\lambda}},
$$
with corresponding density
$$
    f(t) = F'(t) = \frac{\lambda t^{\lambda-1}}{(1+t^{\lambda})^2}
$$
for $t > 0.$  
:::


::: {#def-AFT} 
Let $G$ be a distribution function (on $\mathbb{R}$). The corresponding accelerated failure time (AFT) model 
has survival function given as 
$$
    S_{\eta} (t) = 1 - G( (\log(t) - \eta)/\sigma)
$$
with $\eta = X^T \beta$ the linear predictor and $\sigma > 0$ a scale parameter. 
[The AFT model is a scale-location model of the log-survival time.]{.aside}
:::

The interpretation of the AFT model is that a 
unit change of the $j$-th predictor, with the other predictors fixed, multiplies the
failure time by a factor $e^{\beta_j}.$ The predictor thus changes the time scale, and 
it *accelerates* ($\beta_j < 0$) or decelerates ($\beta_j > 0$) the time to failure. 


::: {#exm-log-logistic-II}

## Log-logistic AFT model

If $G(z) = e^z/(1 + e^z)$ is the standard logistic distribution function and the scale parameter is $\sigma = \lambda^{-1},$
the survival function for the corresponding AFT model is 
$$
        \begin{aligned}
            S_{\eta}(t)  & = \frac{1}{1 + e^{\lambda(\log(t) - \eta)}} \\
            & = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\lambda \eta} t^{\lambda}}.
        \end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-log-logistic-surv}
where $\eta = X^T \beta$ is the linear predictor. This is 
a log-logistic distribution as introduced in @exm-log-logistic. The 
effect of $\eta$ is[^scaling] a *scale transformation* of the log-logistic 
distribution with scale parameter $e^{\eta}.$ The density is 
$$
    \begin{aligned}
        f_{\eta}(t) & = \frac{\lambda e^{-\lambda \eta} t^{\lambda-1}}{(1+e^{-\lambda \eta} t^{\lambda})^2} \\
        & = \frac{\lambda e^{\lambda (\log(t) - \eta)} t^{-1}}{(1+e^{\lambda(\log(t)  - \eta)})^2}.
    \end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-log-logistic-dens}

[^scaling]: If $T$ has log-logistic distribution with density $f_0,$ then $e^{\eta} T$ is log-logistic distributed with density $f_{\eta},$ cf. @exr-loglog. 
::: 

\index{accelerated failure time} 

For maximum likelihood estimation 
we need to compute and optimize the likelihood in @eq-survlike. Efficient 
computation requires access to the density as well as the survival function. 
Both are explicitly available for the log-logistic distribution, 
which makes this distribution attractive for AFT models. 

::: {#exm-log-logistic-prostate}

We implement the negative log-likelihood (`nll()`) for the AFT model with 
a log-logistic survival distribution below. The implementation is 
based on @eq-survlike using the expressions ([-@eq-log-logistic-surv])
and ([-@eq-log-logistic-dens]) for the survival function and density, 
respectively, of the log-logistic distribution. 

The `nll()` function takes four arguments. Besides a vector of parameters (`par`),
the censored survival times (`time`) and the status indicator (`status`), it 
takes a single additional argument `x` representing a categorical variable 
with $k$ values. The parameter vector `par` is of the form 
$$
    (\sigma, \beta_0, \ldots, \beta_{k-1}) = (\lambda^{-1}, \beta_0, \ldots, \beta_{k-1})
$$
with $\sigma$ the scale parameter, $\beta_0$ the intercept and $\beta_1, \ldots, \beta_{k-1}$ 
are contrasts. The survival function is also implemented below for later usage.

```{r}
#| label: log-logistic-log-likelihood
#| code-fold: show
# Argument `x` is an integer representing the k levels of a single 
# categorical predictor variable. `par[2:(k+1)]` are the k 
# beta-parameters corresponding to the intercept and contrasts. 
# Its default value corresponds to no predictor.
nll <- function(par, time, status, x = rep(1, length(time))) {
    lambda <- 1 / par[1]
    eta <- par[2] + c(0, par[-c(1, 2)])[x] # beta_x
    uncens <- status == 1
    lt <- log(time)
    logf <- (log(lambda) - lambda * eta[uncens] + (lambda - 1) * lt[uncens] - 
        2 * log(1 + exp(lambda * (lt[uncens] - eta[uncens])))) |> sum()
    neg_logS <- log(1 + exp(lambda * (lt[!uncens] - eta[!uncens]))) |> sum()
    - logf + neg_logS
}
```

We use `optim()` with method `L-BFGS-B` to compute the maximum-likelihood estimate
of a single survival distribution. Since some of the patients have survived less 
than one month, some survival times are registered as $0,$ which is 
numerically problematic (due to $\log(0)$). For this reason we add 
$0.5$ to all times, corresponding to shifting all survival and censoring times by half a month.

```{r}
#| label: log-logistic-optim
#| code-fold: show
prostate_aft <- optim(
    c(2, 2), 
    nll, 
    method = "L-BFGS-B", 
    lower = c(0.01, -Inf),
    time = prostate$dtime + 0.5, # to avoid log(0)
    status = prostate$status != "alive"
)
prostate_aft[1:2]
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-log-logistic-prostate
#| fig-cap: "The survival function for the fitted log-logistic distribution (blue) and the Kaplan-Meier estimator (black)."
#| column: margin
#| echo: false
#| opts.label: smallfigure
S <- function(t, sigma, eta) 1 / (1 + exp((log(t) - eta) / sigma))
fit <- tibble(time = 0:80, surv = S(time + 0.5, prostate_aft$par[1], prostate_aft$par[2]))
summary(prostate_KM, data.frame = TRUE) |> 
        ggplot(aes(time + 0.5, surv)) + 
        geom_step() +
        geom_line(data = fit, color = "blue") + 
        ylim(0, 1) +
        xlab("time (months)") + 
        ylab("survival probability")

```


We see from the `optim()` result that the parameter estimates are $\hat{\sigma} =$ `r round(prostate_aft$par[1], 2)`
and $\hat{\beta}_0 =$  `r round(prostate_aft$par[2], 2)`, and 
we can also see that $-\ell(\hat{\sigma}, \hat{\beta}_0) =$ `r round(prostate_aft$value, 2)`.
The corresponding fitted survival function is compared to the Kaplan-Meier 
estimator in @fig-log-logistic-prostate.

We can also use our implementation to fit the regression model where the 
survival distribution depends on treatment.

```{r}
#| label: log-logistic-optim-rx
#| code-fold: show
prostate_aft_rx <- optim(
    c(2, 2, 0, 0, 0), 
    nll, 
    method = "L-BFGS-B", 
    lower = c(0.1, -Inf, -Inf, -Inf, -Inf),
    time = prostate$dtime + 0.5, # to avoid log(0)
    status = prostate$status != "alive", 
    x = as.numeric(prostate$rx)
)
prostate_aft_rx[1:2]
```



```{r}
#| label: fig-prostate-aft-rx
#| fig-cap: "The AFT survival functions for the fitted log-logistic distributions (solid) and the Kaplan-Meier estimators (dashed) for each of the four treatment groups."
#| fig-cap-location: margin
# The log-logistic survival function in the scale-location parametrization. 
time0 <- 0:80
fit <- tibble(
    time = rep(time0, 4), 
    surv = c(
        S(time0 + 0.5, prostate_aft_rx$par[1], prostate_aft_rx$par[2]),
        S(time0 + 0.5, prostate_aft_rx$par[1], prostate_aft_rx$par[2] + prostate_aft_rx$par[3]),
        S(time0 + 0.5, prostate_aft_rx$par[1], prostate_aft_rx$par[2] + prostate_aft_rx$par[4]),
        S(time0 + 0.5, prostate_aft_rx$par[1], prostate_aft_rx$par[2] + prostate_aft_rx$par[5])
    ),
    strata = rep(paste("rx=", levels(prostate$rx), sep = ""), each = 81)
)

summary(prostate_KM_rx, data.frame = TRUE) |> 
        ggplot(aes(time + 0.5, surv, color = strata)) + 
        geom_step(linetype = 2) +
        geom_line(data = fit) + 
        ylim(0, 1) +
        xlab("time (months)") + 
        ylab("survival probability") +
        theme(legend.position = "top")
```
:::

We can fit AFT models, and a range of other parametric regression models, via the 
`survreg()` function from the survival package. 

```{r}
#| label: prostate-survreg-rx
#| echo: true
survreg(
    Surv(dtime + 0.5, status != "alive") ~ rx, 
    data = prostate, 
    dist = "loglogistic"
)
```

Note that the parametrization used by `survreg()` is exactly the same as we implemented, 
and that the estimated parameter values and computed log-likelihood are the same as well
(up to small numerical differences). 

The `survreg()` function even gives a likelihood-ratio test statistic (`Chisq`) of the hypothesis 
that there are no differences between the treatments. The corresponding 
$p$-value is computed using an approximating $\chi^2$-distribution with 
$3$ degrees of freedom. It is above $0.1$ and we cannot reject that 
there is no treatment effect. 

As for `lm` and `glm` objects there are methods for `survreg` objects implemented 
in the broom package for the `glance()` and `tidy()` functions and in the survival 
package for `anova()`. We will illustrate some of their usages in subsequent examples.

#### Proportional hazards models {.unnumbered}

A different model class is given by letting the linear predictor have
a multiplicative effect on the hazard function. The resulting 
proportional hazards models are among the most widely 
used survival models. 

\index{proportional hazards model} \index{baseline hazard}

::: {#def-prop-hazard} 
With $\lambda_0$ a baseline hazard function, the proportional hazards model 
is given by the hazard function
$$
    \lambda(t) = \lambda_0(t) e^{\eta}
$$
with $\eta$ the linear predictor. 
:::

It follows that for the cumulative hazard function, 
$$
    \Lambda(t) = \Lambda_0(t) e^{\eta},
$$
and the proportionality holds for the cumulative hazard as well. 
The factor $e^{\beta_j}$ is the *hazard ratio* \index{hazard ratio} between two individuals
whose $j$-th predictors differ by one unit while all other predictors are equal.

The proportional hazards model is sometimes called the *Cox model*. 
@Cox:1972 discovered that for the proportional hazards model, 
the parameters that enter into the linear predictor can be estimated 
without specifying the baseline hazard function. This will be covered in @sec-semipar-surv. 
Here we will instead show how the parameters 
can be estimated via maximum-likelihood when the baseline is assumed to 
be a Weibull distribution. 

::: {#exm-weibull-prop}
The Weibull baseline hazard function and cumulative hazard function are  
$$
    \lambda_0(t) = \gamma t^{\gamma-1} \quad  \text{and} \quad \Lambda_0(t) = t^{\gamma}.
$$
The log-likelihood is 
$$
    \begin{align*}
    \ell & = \sum_{i=1}^n \delta_i \log(\gamma T_i^{\gamma-1}e^{\eta_i}) - T_i^{\gamma}e^{\eta_i} \\ 
    & = \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n \delta_i \log(T_i^{\gamma}e^{\eta_i}) - T_i^{\gamma}e^{\eta_i}}_{\text{Poisson log-likelihood}} + 
    \sum_{i=1}^n \delta_i \log(\gamma T_i^{-1}).
    \end{align*}
$$
This is (surprisingly) up to a constant the log-likelihood for a
Poisson model of the $\delta_i$-s with logarithmic link function and mean value 
$T_i^{\gamma}e^{\eta_i}$ for fixed $\gamma.$ Note that the $\alpha$ parameter 
appearing in @exm-weibull-hazard is captured by an intercept in the linear predictor.

For a fixed value of the linear predictor we also find that 
$$
    \partial_{\gamma} \ell = \sum_{i=1}^n (\delta_i- T_i^{\gamma} e^{\eta_i}) \log T_i + \frac{\delta_i}{\gamma}.
$$
Thus $\gamma$ solves the equation
$$
    \gamma = \frac{n_u}{\sum_{i=1}^n (T_i^{\gamma} e^{\eta_i} -\delta_i)\log T_i}
$$ {#eq-gamma-mle}
with $n_u$ the number of uncensored observations.
[A practical algorithm can alternate between: i) estimate the linear predictor 
as $\hat{\eta}^{(k)}$ by optimizing the Poisson log-likelihood (for fixed 
$\gamma^{(k-1)}$); and ii) update
$$
    \gamma^{(k)} = \frac{n_u}{\sum_{i=1}^n (T_i^{\gamma^{(k-1)}} e^{\hat{\eta}_i^{(k)}} -\delta_i)\log T_i}.
$$
]{.aside}
::: 

The example above shows how implementations of generalized linear models---
and Poisson regression models, in particular---
can be used to fit the Weibull proportional hazards model (for fixed $\gamma$)
with the survival times entering as an offset term. This was of historical 
importance as it made computations practical early on using some standard 
algorithms available. Today, the connection between the survival likelihood 
for Weibull distributions and the Poisson likelihood
is mostly of theoretical and historical interest.

To fit the model we will instead show that the proportional hazards model with a Weibull baseline 
hazard function is also an accelerated failure time model, which makes it possible to 
use `survreg()` to fit the model. 

::: {#exm-weibull-aft}

If we take $G$ in @def-AFT to be the extreme value distribution 
$$
    G(z) = 1 - \exp(-e^{z}),
$$ 
then the corresponding AFT model has survival function 
$$
    S_\eta(t) = \exp\left(-(e^{-\eta}t)^{\frac{1}{\sigma}}\right) = \exp\left(-e^{-\gamma \eta}t^\gamma\right)
$$
where $\gamma = \frac{1}{\sigma}.$ That is, the cumulative hazard function is 
$\Lambda_\eta(t) = e^{- \gamma \eta}t^\gamma,$ which is the proportional hazards 
model with a Weibull baseline, but reparametrized in terms of the scale 
parameter $\sigma = \frac{1}{\gamma},$ and the linear predictor is 
multiplied by $-\gamma.$ 

We can use the `survreg()` function to fit the model. 

```{r}
#| label: tbl-prostate-weibull
#| tbl-cap: "Parameter estimates for the Weibull accelerated failure time model fitted to the prostate cancer survival data."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
#| code-fold: show
prostate_survreg <- survreg(
    Surv(dtime + 0.5, status != "alive") ~ rx, 
    data = prostate, 
    dist = "weibull"
)
prostate_survreg |> tidy()
```

We can compute the estimated survival functions for the Weibull model 
much in the same way as we did above for the log-logistic model, where 
we used the MLE of the parameters and the explicit formula for the 
survival function. However, this is a bit cumbersome and does not generalize 
well. We can instead use the `predict()` method for `survreg` objects 
to predict quantiles for the survival functions, which implicitly also 
gives the estimated survival functions.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: false
S <- function(t, sigma, eta) exp( - exp((log(t) - eta) / sigma))
beta <- coef(prostate_survreg)

time0 <- 0:80
fit <- tibble(
    time = rep(time0, 4), 
    surv = c(
        S(time0 + 0.5, prostate_survreg$scale, beta[1]),
        S(time0 + 0.5, prostate_survreg$scale, beta[1] + beta[2]),
        S(time0 + 0.5, prostate_survreg$scale, beta[1] + beta[3]),
        S(time0 + 0.5, prostate_survreg$scale, beta[1] + beta[4])
    ),
    strata = rep(paste("rx=", levels(prostate$rx), sep = ""), each = 81)
)

summary(prostate_KM_rx, data.frame = TRUE) |> 
        ggplot(aes(time + 0.5, surv, color = strata)) + 
        geom_step(linetype = 2) +
        geom_line(data = fit) + 
        ylim(0, 1) +
        xlab("time (months)") + 
        ylab("survival probability") +
        theme(legend.position = "top") +
        xlim(0, 82)
```


```{r}
#| label: fig-prostate-weibull-rx
#| fig-cap: "The survival functions for the fitted Weibull distributions (solid) and the Kaplan-Meier estimators (dashed) for each of the four treatment groups."
#| fig-cap-location: margin
fit <- tibble(rx = factor(1:4, labels = levels(prostate$rx)))
p_seq <- seq(0.01, 0.90, 0.01)
pred <- predict(prostate_survreg, newdata = fit, type = "quantile", p = p_seq)
fit <- cbind(fit, as_tibble(pred, .name_repair = "minimal")) |> 
    pivot_longer(cols = !rx, values_to = "time") |>
    mutate(
        surv = 1 - rep(p_seq, 4),
        strata = paste("rx=", rx, sep = "")
    ) |> 
    filter(time <= 80)

summary(prostate_KM_rx, data.frame = TRUE) |> 
        ggplot(aes(time + 0.5, surv, color = strata)) + 
        geom_step(linetype = 2) +
        geom_line(data = fit, aes(time)) + 
        ylim(0, 1) +
        xlab("time (months)") + 
        ylab("survival probability") +
        theme(legend.position = "top") +
        xlim(0, 82)
```

@fig-prostate-weibull-rx compares the fitted Weibull distributions to the 
Kaplan-Meier estimators for the four treatment groups, and @tbl-prostate-weibull-test 
reports the test statistic and $p$-value for testing if there are no 
differences between the four treatment groups. The $p$-value is $0.02$ and 
a bit smaller than when using the log-logistic distribution.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-prostate-weibull-test
#| tbl-cap: "Deviance (likelihood-ratio) test of the hypothesis that there are no differences between the four treatment groups."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
#| column: margin
prostate_survreg |> 
    anova() |> 
    select(-4) |> 
    tidy() |> 
    filter(term == "rx") |> 
    knitr::kable(digits = 3)
``` 

To corroborate the technical relation between the log-linear Poisson regression model and 
the proportional hazards model with a Weibull baseline, we refit the $\beta$-parameters
using `glm()` (fixing the scale parameter at its estimated value).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-prostate-glm
#| tbl-cap: "Regression parameters estimated using `glm()` and identical to those in @tbl-prostate-weibull."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
#| code-fold: show
sigma <- prostate_survreg$scale
glm((status != "alive") ~ offset(log(dtime + 0.5) / sigma) + rx, 
    data = prostate, 
    family = "poisson"
) |> coefficients() * (- sigma)
```
:::

To conclude our analyses of the prostate survival times, we have shown how one 
treatment group (1.0 mg estrogen) has a slightly different survival distribution 
than the other three with a better survival prognosis. For the statistical tests 
of any treatment effect, based on two parametric models, only one is significant.
The signal is therefore weak and we cannot draw a clear conclusion on whether there 
is a treatment effect. 

There does not seem to be any detectable difference between the other three treatment groups. 
It is particularly noteworthy that the treatment group with the highest dose (5.0 mg estrogen)
has a survival distribution similar to the placebo group. If there were an effect, we 
would often expect it to be monotone in dosage, and it would be peculiar if the effect is 
only there for the medium dose. 

## Semiparametric survival models {#sec-semipar-surv}

For the parametric proportional hazards models in @def-prop-hazard, the baseline 
hazard function $\lambda_0$ is either known or parametrized itself. Since any 
specific parametrized baseline model might be misspecified, we would like to avoid 
modeling the baseline hazard if possible. This leads to the semiparametric proportional 
hazards model, where an individual's hazard is proportional to a 
common baseline hazard $\lambda_0$ with the individual relative risk as proportionality factor, 
but where we do not model[^semi] the baseline $\lambda_0.$ 

[^semi]: This is similar to *not* making distributional assumptions such as A3 or GA3 for the linear and generalized linear models.

The general proportional hazards model assumes that the 
dependence on the predictors is via a multiplicative factor on the baseline, 
and the $i$-th individual thus has hazard function
$$
    \lambda_i(t) = \psi_i \lambda_0(t)
$$
for $\psi_i > 0$ the *relative risk*[^relrisk] \index{relative risk} of the $i$-th individual. The cumulative hazard function is consequently $\Lambda_i(t) = \psi_i \Lambda_0(t).$

In the following sections we discuss parametrization and estimation of the relative risks
via maximization of Cox's partial likelihood. This is an estimation criterion based on the 
full likelihood but where the baseline hazard has been profiled out. 


[^relrisk]: The $i$-th relative risk could be $e^{\eta_i}$ with $\eta_i = X_i^T \beta$ the linear predictor, but it does not need to be for the general arguments.

### Cox's partial likelihood

[To ease notation we leave out limits on generic indices $i$ and $j$ in products and sums. They will always run through observations from $1$ to $n.$]{.aside}

::: {#def-cum-weight} 
In terms of the observations $T_1, \ldots, T_n$ and relative risks $\psi_1, \ldots, \psi_n > 0$ we 
define the cumulative relative risk process 
$$
    \Psi(t) = \sum_{j: t \leq T_j} \psi_j
$$ 
and the cumulative relative risks $\Psi_i = \Psi(T_i).$
:::


\index{Cox's partial likelihood} \index{partial likelihood}

::: {#def-cox-likelihood}
Cox's partial likelihood for the proportional hazards model[^ties-partial-likelihood] is 
$$
    L_{\mathrm{par}} (\Psi) = \prod_{i: \delta_i = 1} \frac{\psi_i}{\Psi_i}
$$
where the cumulative relative risks $\Psi_i$ are given by @def-cum-weight.
::: 

[^ties-partial-likelihood]: If there are no ties among the outcome observations in the data, the relative risks $\psi_i$ are determined uniquely by the jumps of $\Psi$. If there are ties, we cannot disentangle the individual relative risks completely from $\Psi$ alone. We write $L_{\mathrm{par}}$ as a function of $\Psi$ anyway for notational convenience, remembering that when there are ties, $\Psi$ must be annotated with information about how the jumps decompose into relative risk contributions for each individual. 

The partial likelihood is a function of the relative risks only, but its definition
may appear somewhat unmotivated. The following proposition shows how it is related to 
the survival likelihood.


::: {#prp-fac2}
When $\Lambda_i(t) = \psi_i \Lambda_0(t)$ the survival likelihood equals
$$
    L(\Psi, \Lambda_0) \coloneqq  L_{\mathrm{par}} (\Psi) \left(\prod_{i} 
    (\Psi_i \lambda_0(T_i))^{\delta_i}\right) e^{-\int_0^{\infty} \Psi(t) \lambda_0(t) \mathrm{d} t}.
$$
::: 

::: {.proof}
First note that with $\Psi(t) = \sum_{j: t \leq T_j} \psi_j,$
$$
    \sum_{i} \Lambda_i(T_i) = \int_0^{\infty} \Psi(t) \lambda_0(t) \mathrm{d} t.
$$
The survival likelihood can therefore be factorized as  
$$
    \begin{align*}
      L(\Lambda) & = \prod_{i} \lambda_i(T_i)^{\delta_i} e^{-\Lambda_i(T_i)} \\
        & = \left(\prod_{i: \delta_i = 1} (\psi_i \lambda_0(T_i))^{\delta_i}\right) e^{-\int_0^{\infty} \Psi(t) \lambda_0(t)
        \mathrm{d} t} \\ 
        & = \prod_{i: \delta_i = 1} \frac{\psi_i}{\Psi_i} \left(\prod_{i} 
        (\Psi_i \lambda_0(T_i))^{\delta_i}\right) e^{-\int_0^{\infty} \Psi(t) \lambda_0(t)
        \mathrm{d} t} =  L(\Psi, \Lambda_0).
    \end{align*}
$$
:::


@prp-fac2 decomposes the likelihood into two factors
$$
    L(\Psi, \Lambda_0) =  L_{\mathrm{par}} (\Psi)  \tilde{L}(\Psi, \Lambda_0), 
$$
where the second factor is 
$$
    \tilde{L}(\Psi, \Lambda_0) = 
    \left(\prod_{i} (\Psi_i \lambda_0(T_i))^{\delta_i}\right) e^{-\int_0^{\infty} \Psi(t) \Lambda_0(\mathrm{d} t)}.
$$
It is only this second factor that depends on the baseline hazard. A standard idea is then 
to compute the *profile likelihood* by maximizing $\tilde{L}(\Psi, \Lambda_0)$ 
over $\Lambda_0$ for a fixed cumulative relative risk process $\Psi.$ 
This is, unfortunately, not directly possible, since $\tilde{L}(\Psi, \Lambda_0)$
can be driven to $+ \infty$ if we maximize over 
$\Lambda_0$---even if $\Lambda_0$ is constrained to be given by a continuous hazard function $\lambda_0$. 
It is, however, possible to *renormalize* the factor such that the 
profiling operation can be carried out in a meaningful way.  

Given $\varepsilon > 0$, the *renormalized likelihood factor* is defined as 
$$ 
    \tilde L_\varepsilon(\Psi, \Lambda_0) = \prod_i \Big(\Psi_i\,\big[\Lambda_0(T_i) - \Lambda_0(T_i-\varepsilon)\big]\Big)^{\delta_i} e^{-\int_0^\infty \Psi(t)\,\Lambda_0(\mathrm{d} t)}.
$$
For a continuously differentiable $\Lambda_0$, 
$$
    \Lambda_0(T_i)-\Lambda_0(T_i-\varepsilon) = \varepsilon \lambda_0(T_i) + o(\varepsilon),
$$
whence if $\lambda_0(T_i) > 0$ for all uncensored observations,
$$
    \tilde L_\varepsilon(\Psi, \Lambda_0) = \varepsilon^{n_u}\,\tilde L(\Psi, \Lambda_0)\,(1+o(1)),
$$
where $n_u \coloneqq \sum_{i} \delta_i$ is the number of uncensored observations. 


::: {#prp-profiling}
If there are no ties in the data and $\varepsilon > 0$ is smaller than the smallest gap between 
distinct observation times, then 
$$
    \sup_{\Lambda_0} \tilde L_\varepsilon(\Psi, \Lambda_0) = e^{-n_u}
$$ {#eq-profiling}
and the supremum is attained in 
$$
    \hat{\Lambda}_0(t) = \sum_{i: T_i \leq t} \frac{\delta_i}{\Psi_i}. 
$$
[The supremum in @eq-profiling is taken over *all* cumulative hazard functions $\Lambda_0$,
regarded as distribution functions for measures, including 
*jump cumulative hazard functions* of the form 
$$
    \Lambda_0(t) = \sum_{i : T_i \leq t} \lambda_i
$$
for $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n \geq 0$. These are measures 
with point masses $\lambda_i$ in $T_i,$ 
that is, $\Delta \Lambda_0(T_i) = \lambda_i.$]{.aside}
:::

::: {.proof}
The cumulative relative risk process $\Psi$ is a left-continuous step function 
that is constant between observation times. So $\Psi(s) = \Psi_i$ for 
$s \in (T_i-\varepsilon,T_i]$. 

With $\omega_i = \Lambda_0(T_i) - \Lambda_0(T_i - \varepsilon)$,
$$
    \int_0^\infty \Psi(t) \,\Lambda_0(\mathrm{d}t) \ge \sum_i \Psi_i \omega_i,
$$
with equality exactly when $\Lambda_0$ puts no mass outside the windows 
$(T_i-\varepsilon,T_i]$ on the set where $\Psi > 0$. 

This shows that 
$$
    \log\tilde L_\varepsilon(\Psi, \Lambda_0) \le \sum_i \big(\delta_i\log(\Psi_i \omega_i) - \Psi_i \omega_i\big).
$$
The right-hand side is maximized term by term when 
$$
    \hat{\omega}_i = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 
    \Psi_i^{-1} & \quad \text{if } \delta_i = 1 \\
    0 & \quad \text{if } \delta_i = 0.
     \end{array}\right.
$$
This maximum is attained for $\hat{\Lambda}_0$ with 
$$
     \log\tilde L_\varepsilon(\Psi, \hat{\Lambda}_0) = - \sum_{i} \delta_i = - n_u. 
$$
:::

We conclude from @prp-fac2 and @prp-profiling that for $\varepsilon$ small,
$$
\begin{align*}
L(\Psi, \Lambda_0) & =  L_{\mathrm{par}} (\Psi)  \tilde{L}(\Psi, \Lambda_0) \\
& \approx L_{\mathrm{par}} (\Psi) \tilde{L}_{\varepsilon}(\Psi, \Lambda_0) \ \varepsilon^{-n_u},
\end{align*}
$$
with the approximation holding for any fixed $\Lambda_0(t) = \int_0^t \lambda_0(s) \mathrm{d} s$ 
as $\varepsilon \to 0$. Fixing (a small) $\varepsilon > 0$ and maximizing the renormalized 
likelihood factor over $\Lambda_0$ gives 
$$
L_{\mathrm{par}} (\Psi) e^{-n_u} \varepsilon^{-n_u},
$$
which is Cox's partial likelihood up to the factor $e^{-n_u} \varepsilon^{-n_u}$ that 
depends on neither the baseline nor the relative risks. 

Note that the supremum in @eq-profiling is, for any sufficiently small 
$\varepsilon > 0$, also attained by any $\Lambda_0^{\varepsilon}$ 
with hazard function $\lambda_0^{\varepsilon}$ fulfilling $\lambda_0^{\varepsilon}(s) = 0$
for $s \not \in \cup_i (T_i-\varepsilon,T_i]$ and 
$$
    \int_{T_i - \varepsilon}^{T_i} \lambda_0^{\varepsilon}(s) \mathrm{d} s = \hat{\omega}_i.
$$
Each of these converges pointwise to $\hat{\Lambda}_0$ for $\varepsilon \to 0$, and 
$\hat{\Lambda}_0$ is sensibly regarded as *the* nonparametric maximum-likelihood 
estimate of $\Lambda_0$. 

### Estimation and inference 

The arguments following @prp-fac2 and @prp-profiling show that for estimation 
of parameters that enter into the relative risks[^var-ind2], and not into 
$\lambda_0,$ we can ignore the factor $\tilde{L}(\Psi, \Lambda_0)$ in 
the likelihood and simply optimize the partial likelihood.

[^var-ind2]: And are variation independent of $\lambda_0.$

In practice, the relative risks are typically linked to a vector of predictors 
$X$ via an exponential function, that is, they are of the form
$$
    \psi_i = e^{X^T_i \beta} = e^{\eta_i}.
$$ {#eq-exp-weights}
In this case we find that the partial log-likelihood equals   
$$
    \ell_{\mathrm{par}}(\beta) = \log L_{\mathrm{par}}(\beta) = 
    \sum_{i: \delta_i = 1} X_i^T \beta - \log \Bigg(\underbrace{\sum_{j: T_i \leq T_j} \psi_j}_{\Psi_i} \Bigg),
$$ {#eq-partial-ll}
with corresponding score function 
$$
    \begin{aligned}
    \mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{par}}(\beta) & = \nabla \ell_{\mathrm{par}}(\beta) = 
        \sum_{i: \delta_i = 1} \left( X_i - \sum_{j: T_i \leq T_j} \frac{\psi_j}{\Psi_i} X_j \right) \\
        & = \sum_{i: \delta_i = 1} \left( X_i - \bar{X}_i \right),
    \end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-partial-score}
where 
$$
    \bar{X}_i =  \sum_{j: T_i \leq T_j} \frac{\psi_j}{\Psi_i}  X_j.
$$
The information function becomes 

$$
    \begin{aligned}
      \mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{par}}(\beta) & = - D \mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{par}}(\beta) \\
        & = \sum_{i: \delta_i = 1} \left( \sum_{j: T_i \leq T_j} \frac{\psi_j}{\Psi_i} X_j X_j^T  - 
        \bar{X}_i \bar{X}_i^T \right) \\
        & = \sum_{i: \delta_i = 1} \sum_{j: T_i \leq T_j} \frac{\psi_j}{\Psi_i} (X_j - \bar{X}_i)(X_j - 
         \bar{X}_i)^T, 
    \end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-partial-information}
where we have used that the sum of the weights $\psi_j / \Psi_i$ for $j$ with $T_i \leq T_j$ is one.


The estimate, $\hat{\beta},$ is computed by maximizing $\ell_{\mathrm{par}},$ and 
the observed information, $\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{par}}(\hat{\beta}),$ is used for quadratic approximations 
of $\ell_{\mathrm{par}},$ for standard error estimates and Wald tests. In practice, the computations 
proceed just as if $\ell_{\mathrm{par}}$ were a log-likelihood function. 

The particular score test
$$
    \mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{par}}(0)^T \mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{par}}(0)^{-1} \mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{par}}(0)
$$
for testing $\beta = 0$ reduces to a classical test known as the *log-rank test* \index{log-rank test} 
in the special case with only a single categorical predictor and no ties.  

::: {#exm-prostate-coxph}
Cox's proportional hazards model can be fitted to data via the function `coxph()` 
from the survival R package. 

```{r}
#| label: tbl-prostate-cox
#| tbl-cap: "Estimated regression parameters for Cox's proportional hazards model for the prostate cancer survival data."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
#| code-fold: show
prostate_cox <- coxph( 
    Surv(dtime + 0.5, status != "alive") ~ rx, 
    data = prostate, 
)
prostate_cox |> tidy()
```


```{r}
#| label: tbl-prostate-cox-test
#| tbl-cap: "Likelihood-ratio test of the hypothesis of no treatment effect."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
#| column: margin
anova(prostate_cox) |> 
    tidy() |> 
    filter(term == "rx") |> 
    knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```


```{r}
#| label: cox-survdiff-comp
#| eval: false
#| echo: false
survdiff(
    Surv(dtime, status != "alive") ~ rx, 
    data = prostate,
)
summary(prostate_cox)
```

The parameter estimates are comparable to those obtained by `survreg()` with the 
Weibull distribution, by appropriately rescaling, since that model is parametrized 
as an AFT model. In particular, the Cox model regression parameters have the opposite 
sign. This is noteworthy, since a negative value of a Cox model regression parameter 
means that the corresponding predictor has a positive association with the survival time. 
That is, if $\beta_j < 0$ then a unit increase of the $j$-th predictor multiplies the hazard by the factor
$e^{\beta_j} < 1,$ which results in a survival distribution with longer survival times.

Note that the (partial) likelihood-ratio test reported in @tbl-prostate-cox-test results in a very 
similar conclusion as using the Weibull baseline.
:::

Once we have estimated $\beta$ via the partial likelihood, we can estimate the 
baseline via @prp-profiling. When $\psi_i = e^{X_i^T \beta},$ @prp-profiling results in the estimator
$$
    \hat{\Lambda}_0(t) = \sum_{i: T_i \leq t} \frac{\delta_i}{\sum_{j:T_i \leq T_j} e^{X_j^T \hat{\beta}}}
$$
of the baseline cumulative hazard function in terms of the survival times and the 
estimate $\hat{\beta}.$ This estimator is known as the *Breslow estimator*,
which can be seen as an extension of the Nelson-Aalen estimator of the baseline 
cumulative hazard function. 

\index{Breslow estimator} 

::: {#exm-prostate-breslow}

We continue @exm-prostate-coxph and compute the Breslow estimator of the baseline 
cumulative hazard using `survfit()`, see `?survfit.coxph` for details. 
In fact, `survfit()` returns an estimate of the baseline survival function as
$$
    \hat{S}_0(t) = e^{-\hat{\Lambda}_0(t)}
$$
where $\hat{\Lambda}_0$ is a Breslow-type estimator.


```{r}
#| label: fig-prostate-cox-breslow
#| fig-cap: "The Breslow estimate of the baseline survival function."
#| column: margin
#| code-fold: show
survfit(prostate_cox) |>
    summary(data.frame = TRUE) |>
    ggplot(aes(time, surv)) + 
        geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), fill = "gray90") +
        geom_step() +
        ylim(0, 1) +
        xlab("time (months)") + 
        ylab("survival probability") 
```

@fig-prostate-cox-breslow shows the Breslow estimate including a pointwise 
95% confidence band, which is also computed by the `survfit()` function. 
@fig-prostate-coxph-rx shows the fitted survival functions for the four different
treatment groups, using the Breslow estimator of the baseline cumulative hazard function,
compared to using a Weibull parametric model as baseline. The survival curves are 
based on the Cox model and in principle computed as 
$$
    \hat{S}_k = e^{-e^{\hat{\beta}_k} \hat{\Lambda}_0}, \quad k = 0, 1, 2, 3.
$$ {#eq-mult-baseline}
Note that for Cox's proportional hazards model, $\beta_0 = 0$ always. That is, there is no 
intercept parameter. Since the baseline hazard is nonparametric, we cannot identify a separate 
intercept parameter in this model, and the intercept is effectively absorbed into the nonparametric 
baseline. As pointed out in the  `survfit()` documentation, this also means that there is no 
such thing as *the* baseline hazard. 
What the baseline hazard is depends on a choice of baseline value of $X,$ and thus also 
on how the predictors are encoded. In this example, the 
baseline computed by `survfit()` corresponds to the placebo treatment group, but in more 
complicated setups the baseline corresponds to a pseudo individual---see `?survfit.coxph`. 

It can be instructive to extract the estimated regression parameters and use
([-@eq-mult-baseline]) explicitly, but it is safer and more convenient to compute the 
estimated survival functions shown in @fig-prostate-coxph-rx using `survfit()` with 
a new dataset. The code below shows how, and it gives a survival function for each 
row of the new data. 

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: false
beta <- coefficients(prostate_cox)
summary(prostate_cox_baseline, data.frame = TRUE) |> 
    mutate(
        cumhaz1 = exp(beta[1]) * cumhaz,
        cumhaz2 = exp(beta[2]) * cumhaz,
        cumhaz3 = exp(beta[3]) * cumhaz
    ) |> 
    pivot_longer(
        cols = c(cumhaz, cumhaz1, cumhaz2, cumhaz3), 
        values_to = "cumhaz", 
        names_to = "strata"
    ) |> 
    mutate(
        strata = factor(strata, labels = paste("rx=", levels(prostate$rx), sep = ""))
    ) |>
    mutate(surv = exp(-cumhaz)) |>
    ggplot(aes(time + 0.5, surv, color = strata)) + 
        geom_line(data = fit, aes(time), linetype = 2) +
        geom_step() +
        ylim(0, 1) +
        xlab("time (months)") + 
        ylab("survival probability") +
        theme(legend.position = "top")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-prostate-coxph-rx
#| fig-cap: "The fitted survival functions for proportional hazards models using the Cox proportional hazards model with the Breslow estimator of the baseline (solid, step) and the parametric Weibull survival functions (dashed) for each of the four treatment groups."
#| fig-cap-location: margin
#| message: false
pred_frame <- tibble(
    data = 1:4,
    rx = factor(1:4, labels = levels(prostate$rx)),
    strata = factor(1:4, labels = paste("rx=", rx, sep = ""))
    )
survfit(prostate_cox, newdata = pred_frame) |>
    summary(data.frame = TRUE) |>
    left_join(pred_frame) |>
     ggplot(aes(time, surv, color = strata)) + 
        geom_line(data = fit, linetype = 2) +
        geom_step() +
        ylim(0, 1) +
        xlab("time (months)") + 
        ylab("survival probability") +
        theme(legend.position = "top")
```
:::

### How ties are handled

Some of the results and procedures in the previous sections required no 
ties in the data. In this section we briefly discuss how to handle ties, 
which occur frequently in practice.

If there are ties among the survival times, the summation over $j: T_i \leq T_j$ in the 
definition of the cumulative relative risks is still well defined. If it happens that $T_i = T_k,$ 
the corresponding cumulative relative risks $\Psi_i = \Psi_k$ also become identical.
And if both observations are uncensored, they enter into the partial likelihood 
as the product
$$
    \frac{\psi_i}{\Psi_i} \frac{\psi_k}{\Psi_k} = \frac{\psi_i \psi_k}{\Psi_i^2}.
$$
This implicit way of handling ties is known as Breslow's method. It 
treats ties as if they were really due to events that happened at the exact same time.

The renormalization argument extends to handle ties in this way. To see this, 
suppose there are $d_k$ tied deaths at the $k$-th distinct time, 
where $\Psi$ takes the value $\Psi_{(k)}$. The corresponding window then contributes 
$(\Psi_{(k)}\omega_k)^{d_k} e^{-\Psi_{(k)}\omega_k}$, which is maximized at 
$\omega_k = d_k/\Psi_{(k)}$. This gives 
$$
    \sup_{\Lambda_0} \tilde L_\varepsilon = \prod_k d_k^{d_k}\, e^{-n_u},
$$ 
which is still independent of $\Psi$. The profile is therefore $L_{\mathrm{par}}$ with 
Breslow's tie handling, and the formula for $\hat\Lambda_0$ is unchanged. 

If the tie $T_i = T_k$ was due to rounding or grouping, the contribution 
to the partial likelihood from those two observations should have been one of the two factors:
$$
    \frac{\psi_i \psi_k}{\Psi_i (\Psi_i - \psi_i)} \quad \text{or} \quad \frac{\psi_i \psi_k}{\Psi_k (\Psi_k - \psi_k)}.
$$ {#eq-fac}

We could try to break the tie, e.g., by letting the R function `order()` break ties in whatever 
arbitrary way it chooses depending on the sorting algorithm and the original order of the data.
This naive solution will break all ties but in an unsystematic way, choosing one of the two factors above 
arbitrarily. Breaking ties in this way appears difficult to justify, and we should probably 
only break ties if we actually know and use the correct ordering prior to the rounding. 

\index{ties!Efron's method}

Efron's method[^default] represents instead the "correct but unknown" factor
by an approximation. Efron's approximation for two ties is 
$$
    \frac{\psi_i \psi_k}{\Psi_i (\Psi_i - (\psi_i + \psi_k)/2)} = \frac{\psi_i \psi_k}{\Psi_k (\Psi_k - (\psi_i + \psi_k)/2)}
$$
with similar formulas for more than two ties. The approximation is 
close to the geometric mean of the factors ([-@eq-fac]).

[^default]: The default in `coxph()` for handling ties is Efron's method.

Results rarely depend much on whether Efron's or Breslow's method (or even naive tie breaking) 
is used, but Efron's method is usually preferred if the ties are due to a lack of precision 
and not to a true discrete nature of the survival times. 


## Survival residuals {#sec-res-surv}

Model fit can be assessed for survival regression models just as for generalized 
linear models by means of residuals. There are, of course, several different possible choices. 

### Cox-Snell residuals

Cox-Snell residuals are not really residuals in a classical sense, but a transformation 
of the observed survival times to a set of random variables whose distribution should be 
exponential if the model is correct. They are based on the following result.

::: {#lem-cum-haz-trans}
If $T$ has continuous cumulative hazard function $\Lambda$ 
then  $\Lambda(T)$ is exponentially distributed with rate 1. 
::: 

::: {.proof}
The survival function $S(t) = \exp(-\Lambda(t))$ is continuous, whence  
$$
    S(T) \sim \text{unif}([0,1]).
$$
From this it follows that 
$$
    \mathbf{P}(\Lambda(T) \leq t) = \mathbf{P}(S(T) \geq \exp(-t)) = 1 - \exp(-t)
$$
for $t \geq 0,$ or $\Lambda(T) \sim \text{Exp}(1).$
:::

::: {#def-CS}
With $\hat{\Lambda}_i$ an estimator of the cumulative hazard function for $T_i$ the
Cox-Snell residuals are defined as \index{residual!Cox-Snell}
$$
    \hat{\Lambda}_i(T_i)
$$ {#eq-CS}
for $i = 1, \ldots, n.$ 
::: 

From the lemma above we conclude that if $(T_1, \delta_1), \ldots, (T_n, \delta_n)$ are independently right censored
 survival times  with corresponding cumulative hazard functions $\Lambda_1, \ldots, \Lambda_n,$ then 
$$
    (\Lambda_1(T_1), \delta_1), \ldots, (\Lambda_n(T_n), \delta_n)
$$
are independently right censored i.i.d. exponentially distributed variables. 

If there were no censoring, we would expect the Cox-Snell residuals to follow approximately an
exponential distribution. With censoring the Cox-Snell residuals are expected to 
be approximately independently censored exponentially distributed. We use this 
in practice by estimating the cumulative hazard function for the Cox-Snell residuals 
using, e.g., the Nelson-Aalen estimator or the negative log of the Kaplan-Meier 
estimator. The resulting estimate is then 
compared to the cumulative hazard for the exponential distribution, which
is $\Lambda(t) = t.$ In practice we plot the estimated cumulative 
hazards against the Cox-Snell residuals, which should fall on 
a straight line with slope $1.$ 

### Martingale residuals 

The martingale residuals are defined as \index{residual!martingale}
$$
    \delta_i - \hat{\Lambda}_i(T_i),
$$
and are thus the status indicators minus the Cox-Snell residuals. 
Their usefulness is partly justified by the following result.

::: {#lem-MG}
If $T = \min\{T^*, C\}$ with $T^*$ and $C$ independent and both having continuously
differentiable survival functions it holds that
$$
    \mathbf{E}(\Lambda(T)) = \mathbf{P}(T^* \leq C),
$$ 
where $\Lambda$ is the cumulative hazard function for $T^*.$ 
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $S$ and $H$ denote the survival functions of $T^*$ and $C,$ 
respectively. By integration by parts
$$
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbf{E}(\Lambda(T)) & = - \int_0^{\infty} \Lambda(t) (SH)'(t) \mathrm{d} t =
        \int_0^{\infty} \Lambda'(t) S(t) H(t) \mathrm{d} t \\
        &  = \int_0^{\infty} f(t) H(t) \mathrm{d} t = \mathbf{P}(T^* \leq C).
    \end{align*}
$$
[The survival function for the minimum of the two independent random 
variables $T^*$ and $C$ is the product $SH,$ whence the density of their distribution 
is the negative derivative $-(SH)'.$]{.aside}
:::

@lem-MG holds conditionally on $X$ under independent censoring, and it 
follows, possibly using the tower property of conditional 
expectations, that with $\delta = 1(T^* \leq C),$ 
$$
    \mathbf{E} (\delta - \Lambda(T)) = 0.
$$ {#eq-MG-mean}


Thus if $\hat{\Lambda}_i$ were the true cumulative hazard function, 
the  martingale residuals would have mean zero. 

Now $\hat{\Lambda}_i$ is only an estimate, but if the model fits the data, the martingale residuals should have 
approximately mean $0.$ In the more advanced theory of survival 
analysis they also enjoy a  martingale property, which explains their name. 
Here we will not pursue this, but just observe that we can investigate the model
fit by investigating if the martingale residuals  approximately have  mean $0.$ 
The residuals can be used much as regression residuals to judge overall fit as
well as the fit of how the individual predictor variables enter into the model. 
It should be noted, though, that they by definition have a left-skewed distribution[^mg-dis]
concentrated on $(-\infty, 1).$ 

[^mg-dis]: The martingale residuals are *never* approximately normally distributed!

In addition to the martingale residuals, we also define the *squared-martingale residuals*
as
\index{residual!squared-martingale}
$$
    (\delta_i - \hat{\Lambda}_i(T_i))^2 - \hat{\Lambda}_i(T_i).
$$
@exr-mg-res shows that $\mathbf{E}((\delta - \Lambda(T))^2) = \mathbf{E}(\Lambda(T))$ 
under independent censoring, if $\Lambda$ is the cumulative hazard function for $T^*$, 
and the squared-martingale residuals should thus also roughly have mean zero. 

::: {#exm-prostate-residuals}
As for other regression models, we can use `augment()` from the broom package 
to extract fitted values (the linear predictor) and residuals. @fig-prostate-mg-res-rx
shows the martingale residuals and squared-martingale residuals plotted against 
the treatment (which is the only predictor in the model at this point). 
Since the dataset is rather small, it makes 
sense here to use `geom_beeswarm()` from the ggbeeswarm package to visualize 
the full distribution of the residuals as well as the individual points.
Note the upper cap at $1$ of all martingale residual distributions. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-prostate-mg-res-rx
#| fig-cap: "Martingale (left) and squared-martingale (right) residuals for the Cox model for each of the four treatment groups. The blue points and error bars in the right panel are means and 95% confidence intervals."
#| fig-cap-location: margin
#| opts.label: widefigure2
prostate_cox_aug <- augment(prostate_cox, data = prostate) |>
    mutate(
        Lambda = (status != "alive") - .resid,   # Cox-Snell residuals
        v = .resid^2 - Lambda                    # Squared-martingale residuals
    ) 

p1 <- ggplot(prostate_cox_aug, aes(rx, .resid)) + 
        ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm(alpha = 0.4) +
        ylab("Martingale residuals") +
        theme(
         axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 15, hjust = 1, vjust = 1)
        )
  
p2 <- ggplot(prostate_cox_aug, aes(rx, v)) +
        ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm(alpha = 0.4) +
        geom_point(
            stat = "summary", 
            fun = mean, 
            color = "blue", 
            size = 2.5
        ) + 
        geom_errorbar(
            stat = "summary", 
            fun.data = mean_se, 
            fun.args = list(mult = 1.96),
            color = "blue", 
            width = 0.15, 
            linewidth = 0.7
        ) + 
        ylab("Squared-martingale residuals") +
        theme(
         axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 15, hjust = 1, vjust = 1)
        )

gridExtra::grid.arrange(p1, p2, ncol = 2)
```

Since the model only includes the single categorical predictor `rx`,
the martingale residual plot is not informative about misspecifications,
because the empirical mean of the martingale residuals is forced to be exactly zero within each 
group by the estimation procedure. The plot is only shown here to demonstrate 
what the distribution of martingale residuals looks like. The plot of the
